catalog_quote: Accent is realised by an increase in pitch and a slight increase in length of the stressed syllable. ... The accent always falls on the penultimate syllable. When one or more suffixes are added to a stem the accent shifts to the resulting penultimate syllable. ... When a word seems to be monosyllabic it has a long vowel, which in fact consists of two syllables underlyingly. ... That long vowels are in fact two syllables can be seen in polysyllabic words the last syllable of which has such a lengthened vowel. The stress then falls on the first part of this long vowel, giving the impression that it falls on the final syllable. The same happens with loanwords that originally have a schwa in the penultimate syllable, as well as onomatopoeic words. ... new_statements.quote: Het accent wordt gevormd door de geaccentueerde lettergreep op een hogere toon uitte spreken dan de niet-geaccentueerde, en daaraan een lichte verlenging van de klank te paren. [...] Het accent valt immer op de voorlaatste lettergreep van achteren. Wanneer dus één of meer achtervoegsels of daarmee gelijk te stellen vormen van de voornaamwoorden achter een stamwoord komen, verspringt het accent zoveel lettergrepen naar achteren, als nodig is om het op de voorlaatste te doen vallen. B.v. mangkdbi vragen, mangkabimo al gevraagd hebbende, mangkabikène vraag voor hem [...] (p. 17; Delpher scanned, some accent marks lost in scanned)
new_statements.translation: The accent is formed by pronouncing the accented syllable on a higher tone than the unaccented one, and pairing this with a slight lengthening of the sound. [...] The accent always falls on the penultimate syllable counted from the end. So when one or more suffixes, or pronoun forms to be treated as such, come after a stem, the accent shifts as many syllables rightward as needed to make it fall on the penult. E.g. mangkábi 'to ask', mangkabímo 'having already asked', mangkabikéne 'ask for him' (p. 17)
new_statements.citation: van den Bergh, J.D. 1953. Spraakkunst van het Banggais. 's-Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff (Koninklijk Instituut voor Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde). new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Banggai (qs-tier-2026-09-12) with an EMPTY rule and no existing statements; van den Bergh supplies the placement (fixed penultimate, shifting under suffixation), the phonetic correlates (higher pitch + slight length), secondary accent on the initial syllable of 4+-syllable words, and the exception classes. This fills the gap rather than contradicting anything.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word (stem plus suffixes and enclitic pronouns), realised as higher pitch plus slight lengthening; it shifts rightward under suffixation to stay penultimate. Doubled (long) vowels count as two syllables, so a word-final long vowel takes the stress on its first half and sounds final-stressed (asaang, mopiit). Semi-diphthongs (ai, au, ou, ei) in the last syllable behave as two syllables; in the penult the accent stays on their first vowel and does not shift. West-Peling (fast) speakers reduce unstressed syllables; East-Peling (slow, sing-song) speakers keep them and sometimes show a floating accent over both vowels of a semi-diphthong (aino).
new_statements.secondary_stress: "Vier-lettergrepige woorden krijgen op de eerste lettergreep nog een nevenaccent, dat zwakker is dan het hoofdaccent." (p. 18) — four-syllable words take a secondary accent on the first syllable, weaker than the main accent (pantunggéne, salinsau, kalitátak). "Meer-dan-vier-lettergrepige woorden krijgen eveneens een nevenaccent op de eerste lettergreep en de tussenliggende lettergrepen worden meestal gelijkwaardig uitgesproken." (p. 18) — words of more than four syllables likewise take a secondary accent on the first syllable, with the intervening syllables mostly pronounced alike. "Is echter één van de midden-lettergrepen een semi-tweeklank, dan valt het nevenaccent op de eerste klinker van deze semi-tweeklank." (p. 19) — if a medial syllable is a semi-diphthong the secondary accent falls on its first vowel (konóikène, patáikène).
new_statements.exceptions: "Ook zijn er enkele uitzonderingen, waarbij het accent niet op de voorlaatste lettergreep valt. Zo b.v. langkai man, in eigennamen uitgesproken als langkai: Langkai Piit, Langkai Bengkol." (p. 18) — a few lexical exceptions (langkai 'man' in personal names; sao > saono on West Peling; túboan vs tubóan; East tobúi, babuí from -j). Loanwords with schwa in the penult and onomatopoeic words: "Dus legt men het accent op de laatste lettergeep en verlengt deze. B.v. berkat wordt balakaat, belasting wordt balasitéeng, bangsa wordt banginsaa" (p. 18) — final syllable stressed and lengthened (sanaang, manaang, bateek, kaleek), which the author treats as a true lengthening rather than a departure from the penult rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works treat Banggai (bgz) of the Banggai Archipelago, Central Sulawesi, with an East (Oost-Peling) and a West (West-Peling) dialect. The SIL survey's wordlists come from Adean and Tompudau (east) and Tatabau (west). Van den Bergh states the penultimate rule for the language as a whole and notes dialect differences only in realisation: West-Peling speakers reduce unstressed syllables, East-Peling speakers keep them and sometimes show a floating accent on semi-diphthongs.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding English quotation is verbatim in the held StressTyp2 dump (passage 664, source 513 = van den Bergh 1953, the StressTyp2 entry for this language Banggai; Aki). Deciding source kind: a database paraphrase (2015) of a 1953 Dutch missionary-era grammar sketch; that grammar is nonetheless the best and only description of Banggai stress (Glottolog's single grammar-class ref; no phonology article, JIPA illustration, dissertation or instrumental study found via CrossRef/OpenLibrary/OAPEN/archive.org/Kemdikbud/SIL; the 2019 Indonesian Tata Bahasa gives one paragraph with accent minimal pairs and no rule). sources.quote: Word accent marked by pitch and duration ('nada dan durasi'); minimal pairs by accent position: /polu/ penult-accent 'tungku' vs final-accent 'tidur seranjang', /tutu/ penult 'tumbuk' vs final 'betul'. No default rule stated; consistent with van den Bergh's final-long-vowel analysis (his tutuu 'heel echt').
